title: eToys (1997–2001): the Christmas it overestimated
description: eToys sold toys online from 1997, was worth $7.78 billion after its 1999 IPO and was bankrupt 22 months later, after missing its holiday 2000 forecast.

card.blurb: An Idealab start-up that sold toys online from 1997. Its IPO was valued at $7.78 billion at the first day’s close. It spent more on marketing than it took in gross profit, missed its last Christmas forecast by almost half, and shut down in March 2001.

hero.dates: Website opened October 1997. Chapter 11 filed and site closed Mar 7, 2001.
hero.standfirst: For one day in May 1999 it was worth more than Toys “R” Us. It never once made money.
hero.deck: eToys was an online toy store valued at $7.78 billion at the close of its first trading day in May 1999, and it filed for bankruptcy in March 2001. It was incorporated as Toys.com in November 1996, backed by the incubator Idealab, and began [selling toys online](/category/dotcom/) in October 1997. The IPO priced at $20 and closed its first day at $76.56. To win the 1999 holiday season it spent $55.5M on advertising, built warehouses across the country and lost $189.6M on $151.0M of sales. The next Christmas, sales came in at $131M against a forecast of $210M to $240M. It laid off most of its staff in January 2001 and filed for bankruptcy that March, owing about $274M. Its creditors later sued Goldman Sachs over the IPO price. The facts come from eToys’ [SEC filings](#sources), the court record and contemporary press.

findings.title: Every sale cost more than it earned.
findings.text: In the year to March 2000 marketing and sales expenses were 79.8% of net sales, and gross profit only 19.2% (derived). Advertising alone was $55.5M, 37% of sales.[^1]

findings.title: It built for a Christmas that did not come.
findings.text: It planned a 763,000-square-foot warehouse in Ontario, California and a 715,000-square-foot addition in Virginia.[^1] Holiday 2000 sales were $131.2M; it had forecast $210M to $240M.[^2][^5]

findings.title: It ran out of cash in a closed market.
findings.text: Cash fell from $139.6M in March 2000 to $62.8M by December. The company said it needed “an additional, substantial capital infusion,” blamed “the current disfavor of Internet retailing,” and filed for bankruptcy three months later.[^2][^5][^8]

findings.title: The IPO was the high point.
findings.text: The shares closed at $76.56 on the first day, $25 at the end of 1999, and never again rose above the $20 offering price.[^4][^13]
